approved: Charities (Consequential Amendments and Transitional Provisions) Bill 2013

Mitch Fifield I rise to speak on the Charities Bill 2013 and the Charities (Consequential Amendments and Transitional Provisions) Bill 2013. Acting Deputy President Bishop, I know that I do not need to convince you of the great work that charities do in our community and of the incredible contribution they make to the nation. It is fair to say that Australia would be unrecognisable if the charitable contribution of individuals and of organisations was withdrawn. These organisations really are—it is a cliche but it is true—the glue that holds the community together. They fill in the gaps between what government does, what families do and what businesses do. No government could ever seek to replicate the tremendous good that charities do in our community. I think it is very important that we as a parliament and government more generally are at the service of charities, doing all that can be done to make life easier for charitable organisations rather than making life more difficult. It is for that reason—to avoid making life more difficult for charitable organisations—that the opposition do have misgivings about this legislation. At the heart of the bill is the attempt to seek to introduce a statutory definition of charity and charitable purpose for the purposes of all Commonwealth legislation. This bill in fact represents the first time legislation has sought to comprehensively define charity for the purposes of Commonwealth law. The current definition has been with us for a little while. It is not currently defined in our statutes. Rather, it is the product of over 400 years of common law based on the Statute of Elizabeth. Given the long history of the current definition, the opposition is of the view that if government believes there is good reason to change the definition then the onus is on the government to make the case for a change from the status quo. John Hogg The question now is that the remaining stages of these bills be agreed to and the bills be now passed.

Presented consequential amendments accompanying the Charities Bill 2013, providing transitional registration arrangements with the Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission and preserving the charitable status of entities already recognised as charities.

Opposed the Charities Bill 2013, arguing it unnecessarily replaces a common-law definition of charity dating back more than 400 years to the Statute of Elizabeth with a new statutory definition taking effect 1 January 2014, and recalled the Howard government's more modest 2004 Extension of Charitable Purposes Act as the better approach.

Argued that the Charities Bill 2013 and related transitional legislation would create a statutory definition of charity, improve clarity, reduce duplicated reporting through the Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission, retain common-law flexibility, and support charities and not-for-profits, while commending consultation and Vinnies volunteers.

Argued that the Charities Bill 2013 would replace the common-law definition with complex prescriptive regulation from 1 January 2014, impose further compliance burdens, omit housing as a defined charitable purpose, and risk harming charities, while stating that the coalition would reduce red tape and repeal the legislation.

Argued that the proposed statutory definition of charity from 1 January 2014 was unnecessary, insufficiently consulted on and contrary to 400 years of common law, while opposing the Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission as an added burden and stating that the coalition would repeal the bill and abolish the commission.

Paid tribute to charitable and not-for-profit workers, then argued that the Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission would duplicate regulation, impose unjustified reporting and compliance costs, and hold excessive powers, while questioning the need for a statutory definition after more than 400 years of common law and committing to abolish the commission.

Opposed the Charities Bill 2013, citing the Salvation Army in Townsville getting 81.5 per cent of every donated dollar to front-line services as the model to aim for, and argued the common law definition of charity, used for 400 years since the 1600s, should not be replaced by a new federal bureaucracy.

Opposed the Charities Bill, pledging the coalition would abolish the Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission if elected on 14 September, and recalled that the Howard government's 2000 inquiry into the definition of charity made 27 recommendations before a 2003 draft bill by Treasurer Peter Costello was ultimately not proceeded with.

Opposed the Charities Bill 2013 as an unnecessary expansion of bureaucracy, noting the common law definition of charity has applied since 1601, over 400 years, and pledged the coalition would repeal the legislation if elected on 14 September.

Opposed the Charities Bill 2013, arguing its shift from four to twelve categories of charitable purpose fails to list housing as a defined purpose, citing Waterford shelter Sheltered by Grace turning away about ten homeless people a week and its $100,000 fundraising goal, and calling the changes a red-tape bonanza for the sector.

Opposed the Charities Bill 2013 and its companion bill, quoting Ronald Reagan that government is the problem, and questioned whether a new disqualifying purpose could bar charities that oppose a government decision or a political candidate from registration, citing her own involvement with SIDS and Kids NT and the Cancer Council.

Opposed the Charities Bill 2013, arguing it would overturn 400 years of common law charity definitions dating to the 1891 Pemsel case with little scrutiny, and warned that political advocacy groups such as the Wilderness Society could gain charitable status, citing its campaign against Cape York development opposed by Indigenous leader Noel Pearson.

Opposed the Charities Bill 2013 and its companion bill, arguing the government has shown hostility toward voluntary charitable effort by creating the Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission despite states not agreeing to a single national regulatory layer, and contrasted it with the Howard government's more limited 2004 Extension of Charitable Purpose Act.

Opposed the Charities Bill 2013, arguing local charities are best placed to meet community needs, and criticised the government for announcing in May 2011 that it would give the sector less than two months to accommodate changes originally set to take effect in July 2012.

The Coalition opposed the Charities Bill 2013, warning it could create legal disputes and burden charities, while the Greens supported it after securing clarifications that protect advocacy and environmental purposes. The government argued the bill modernises charity law, reduces red tape, and establishes a single regulatory "passport" for the sector.
